newsitem.title: BELGIUM: ONE-OFF EMU MEASURES NOT ENOUGH - EU REPORT.
newsitem.headline: ONE-OFF EMU MEASURES NOT ENOUGH - EU REPORT.

text.p: The European Commission will say on Thursday that one-off measures taken to help countries meet the requirements of a single currency will not help the objective of sustainable budgetary discipline.

In a report to be released on the European Union's economy, the Commission will also say that it will review the budgets of EU countries in 1998 to see whether durable budgetary convergence has been achieved.
The report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, did not include new forecasts for growth in the EU or the expected pace of budget consolidation in the 15-nation bloc in 1997.
But it says that one-off efforts being used to meet the criteria -- including by Italy and France -- will not help the process of long-lasting budgetary rigour.
"It is evident that the temporary nature of these (types of) measures does not contribute to improving the fundamental budget situation," the report says.
The EU will next week announce its opinion on several budgetary practices governments have employed to bring their deficits down to three percent of gross domestic product, the Maastricht target.
One of the more controversial proposals is Italy's euro tax, a one-time revenue raising measure that some have criticised as being at odds with durable budgetary convergence.
Countries must bring their deficits, inflation and interest rates in line with the Maastricht treaty this year if they hope to qualify for monetary union, expected to start in 1999.
The Commission will announce its revised economic outlook for all 15 nations towards the end of April, incorporating the most recent data from late last year.
Regarding Germany, still Europe's main economic engine, EU officials said it was still too early to tell whether they will have to alter their previous estimates for 1997.

Two important influences are at work: the first is the dampening effects of a somewhat harsher winter and the second the strong dollar, which at a pinch should allow Germany more opportunities for export growth.
During its last round of forecasts in October, the Commission confidently predicted that Germany would bring its 1997 budget deficit down to three percent of GDP, the Maastricht treaty's requirement.

But weaker than expected growth in recent weeks combined with record joblessness have sown doubts among independent analysts on whether Bonn can meet the Maastricht target without further budget cuts.
A Reuter poll of economists suggested on Wednesday that Germany's deficit ratio would be 3.5 percent of GDP this year.
In its annual economic report last month Bonn forecast a deficit ratio of 2.9 percent. A German finance ministry official told Reuters on Wednesday that the rosier estimate still stood.
The Commission's report also highlighted some of the key structural problems facing the EU, such as the competitive effects from an increasingly globalised world economy.
It acknowledged that greater economic integration and rapid advances in technology had contributed partly to the EU's high rate of joblessness.

The study also included an analysis which adjusts the budgetary performance of all 15 nations for the ups and downs in their economies. The upshot of this evaluation is that their budgetary situation may look better than currently forecast.
